title: The Most Meetings That Fit in K Rooms

concept.title: Sort the meetings by their end and give each one the room that became free most recently before its start
body: There are `k` rooms and `n` requested meetings, each from `s` to `e`. A room can host **one meeting at a time**, and a meeting can start when the previous meeting in that room has ended. Which is the **largest number of meetings** that can be held? For the meetings `1-3, 2-4, 3-5, 3-6` and `k = 2` the answer is 3: the meetings 2-4, 3-5 and 3-6 are all running at the time 3.5, so at most two of them fit. With one room this is the classical *activity selection*: sort by the end time and take every meeting that fits.

For `k` rooms keep the **time at which every room becomes free** (all rooms are free at the start). Process the meetings **sorted by their end**. For the meeting `(s, e)` look at the rooms that are free by `s`, that is, whose free time is `<= s`. If there is none, the meeting is skipped. Otherwise put the meeting into the room with the **largest** free time among them: the room that has been idle for the **shortest** time. Its new free time becomes `e`. This "best fit" choice leaves the rooms that have been free for long available for the meetings that start early, which are the most demanding.

body.code:
rooms = [0] * k                       # the free times, sorted
count = 0
for s, e in sorted(meetings, key=lambda m: m[1]):
    i = bisect_right(rooms, s) - 1       # the room with the largest free time <= s
    if i >= 0:
        rooms.pop(i)
        insort(rooms, e)                 # its new free time
        count += 1
print(count)

body: The room list is kept sorted, so finding the room is a binary search and updating it is a removal and an insertion, O(k) each in an array (O(log k) with a balanced tree). The total is O(n log n + n k) with the array. The greedy is correct because a set of meetings can be placed into `k` rooms exactly when no moment is covered by more than `k` of them; "best fit by end time" always builds such a set of maximum size.

statement: `n` meetings (each from `s` to `e`) are requested and there are `k` rooms. A room holds one meeting at a time; a meeting may start at the moment the previous meeting of the room ends. Print the largest number of meetings that can be held.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `k`: the number of meetings and the number of rooms.
Each of the next `n` lines has two numbers `s` and `e`: a meeting that occupies the time from `s` to `e`.
outputFormat: Print the largest number of meetings.
constraints: A room can start a meeting at the moment its previous meeting ends.

examples.note: The meetings 2-4, 3-5 and 3-6 overlap, so only two of them fit; with 1-3 that is 3 (for example 1-3 and 3-5 in one room, 2-4 in the other).
With one room, 2-3 and 4-5 are held: 2.

hints: With one room, sort by end time and take what fits.
Keep the free time of each room in a sorted list.
For a meeting choose the room with the largest free time that is not later than its start.

solution.complexity: Time O(n log n + n k), space O(n + k).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

from bisect import bisect_right, insort

n, k = map(int, input().split())
mt = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

mt.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])
rooms = [0] * k
count = 0
for s, e in mt:
    i = bisect_right(rooms, s) - 1
    if i >= 0:
        rooms.pop(i)
        insort(rooms, e)
        count += 1
print(count)
